The app deletes the oldest backup when there are more than this. It always keeps the newest one. Each device counts only its own backups.
Also keep one a day for a week, one a week for five weeks and one a month for a year

Backups to keep counts the newest backups. With this on, the app also spares some older ones instead of deleting them: the newest backup of each of the last 7 days, of each of the last 5 weeks, and of each of the last 12 months. That is at most 24 more files, and fewer when one backup stands for several of them. A setting you changed by mistake a month ago can then still be taken back, without keeping a month of daily backups to do it. The ages count back from your newest backup, so a phone that stops backing up for a while keeps its old copies until new ones replace them. This setting is off by default.

A second automatic backup beside the main one, with its own schedule, sections and number of copies. Use it for what changes often and is small, like your settings and layouts, every hour or so, and leave the bulky and personal things to the main backup once a day. It goes to the same locations under the same conditions, and pausing backups pauses it too. Its files are named apart, so each kind keeps its own copies, and the restore list shows both. It never includes API keys.
A second, smaller backup on its own schedule, to the same locations
Counted apart from the main backups
With the passphrase under Protect with a passphrase

What goes in a frequent backup
Wait for a connection that costs you nothing

A backup can be a few megabytes, and it goes out every time the timer comes round. With this on, the app waits for Wi-Fi, or for any other connection that Android does not count as metered. With it off, a backup goes out over mobile data as soon as it is due. Folder locations need no connection at all, so this setting only shows when a backup goes to a server or a cloud account. This setting is on by default.
Wait until your device is plugged in

This is what the app always did. Turn it off if you rarely charge your device for long enough, because a backup that never finds a charger never runs, and nothing tells you that it did not. The work itself is a few seconds of copying, so it costs little battery.
The app encrypts each backup. You need the passphrase to restore one.

The app stores the passphrase on this device, because an automatic backup has nobody to type it. This protects the backup file where it goes, for example in a cloud folder. It does not protect it from a person who holds your unlocked device. Write the passphrase down: without it, a backup cannot be restored.

This backup holds words that you typed, text that you copied, or what the AI remembers about you, and no passphrase protects it. The app writes it to your locations on a timer. Turn on a passphrase, or turn off the dictionary, the clipboard, the swipe style and AI memory in What goes in a backup.
